newsitem.title: USA: Jury recesses in Oklahoma bombing case.
newsitem.headline: Jury recesses in Oklahoma bombing case.

text.p: The jury ended deliberations on Sunday without reaching a verdict in the trial of accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, as anxiety grew among waiting survivors and relatives of those killed in the blast.

"I didn't think the jury would have taken this long. That's scary," said Jannie Coverdale, whose grandsons Elijah and Aaron were among the 168 bombing victims. "Somebody on the jury doesn't want to find him guilty."
The jury of seven men and five women asked to stop deliberating at midday on Sunday in order to take a break, Federal Judge Richard Matsch said.

"I'm going to grant your request that you recess deliberations and take the rest of the day off," he said when he called the jury into the Denver federal courtroom at noon. "Rest and relax as much as you can."
He told the sequestered jury, which began deliberations on Friday morning, to resume at 10:30 a.m. EDT (1430 GMT) on Monday.

The jury has spent two-and-a-half days weighing murder and conspiracy charges against McVeigh, 29, a former soldier, who is accused of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995. The explosion killed 168 people and wounded more than 500 others.
He faces the possibility of a death sentence or life in prison if convicted.

McVeigh, wearing an open-necked white shirt, looked relaxed as he sat at the defence table in the courtroom. After the jury recessed, he spent several minutes talking with his chief defence attorney Stephen Jones.
"His mood is good and appropriate for the circumstances now," Jones said later outside the courtroom.
"This is a man that went to war in the Persian Gulf and was in the Army, so he's used to waiting," he added.
Asked if he was concerned about the deliberations heading into another day, the defence attorney said: "I have an opinion about that, but it's probably best if I didn't share it."
Defence attorneys said McVeigh reads and talks on the telephone to friends as he waits in a basement prison cell.
Survivors and family members wait at a church not far from the courthouse, doing crossword puzzles and watching television.

Sponsored by the Justice Department, groups of survivors and relatives have been attending the trial in week-long shifts, and on Sunday, many were preparing to return home to allow another 24-member group to come to Denver.
"I wish the verdict would have come in yesterday so the people that were up here could hear it," said Charles Tomlin, whose son Rick was killed in the explosion.
"They sure wanted to hear it," he said, adding, "Then again, if it was the wrong verdict, they wouldn't want to hear that."
Local defence attorney David Japha, who has followed the trial closely, said he read little or nothing into the length of the deliberations.

"They're looking at each and every element. Did each and every element get proved up beyond a reasonable doubt?" he said. "And if you look at that, they're not really spending an inordinate amount of time."
As the jury deliberated, hundreds of journalists also kept watch at the federal courthouse in Denver, where the testimony in the trial began on April 24.
